specPoints.text: understand, in terms of changes in oxidation number, the following reactions of the halogens: i oxidation reactions with Group 1 and 2 metals ii the disproportionation reaction of chlorine with water and the use of chlorine in water treatment iii the disproportionation reaction of chlorine with cold, dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide to form bleach iv the disproportionation reaction of chlorine with hot alkali v reactions analogous to those specified above

primer.text: Chlorine can fight itself: in alkali and even in water it splits into oxidised and reduced branches at once. This note follows the metal and iron(II) redox routes, then contrasts cold with hot alkali products and shows how drinking water is sterilised by the +1 chlorine branch.

lessons.title: Halogen oxidations of metals and iron(II)
lessons.opening: Hand a halogen a metal and electrons flow: sodium surrenders one per atom to chlorine, calcium two per atom to bromine. Iron(II) solutions reveal a finer ladder - chlorine and bromine lift iron to +3, iodine cannot, and iron(III) even pushes iodide back.
keyPoints: Halogens react with Group 1 and 2 metals to form ionic metal halide salts, with the metal oxidised.
Sodium loses one electron per atom to chlorine; calcium loses two per atom to bromine.
Chlorine and bromine oxidise iron(II) to iron(III), each halogen molecule taking two electrons.
Iodine is too weak an oxidising agent for iron(II); instead iron(III) oxidises iodide back to iodine.

low.restatement: Metals hand electrons to halogens, forming halide salts; among iron(II) solutions the ladder splits: Cl2 and Br2 oxidise Fe2+ to Fe3+, while I2 fails and the reverse reaction with Fe3+ and iodide wins instead.
low.analogy: A strong magnet lifts heavy pins; a weak one cannot - iodine is the weak magnet for iron(II) electrons.
low.examPointer: Learn the iron(II) pair of equations: Cl2/Br2 oxidising Fe2+, and Fe3+ oxidising I- - the reversal is the favourite exam discriminator.

medium.restatement: Each halogen molecule accepts exactly two electrons (one per atom), so two Fe2+ ions are oxidised per halogen molecule; iodine's weaker electron capture leaves Fe2+ untouched, and Fe3+ instead strips iodide of electrons.
medium.analogy: Two ports feed one ship: each halogen molecule docks two electrons, one per atom aboard.
medium.examPointer: Check the electron ledger balances in every half-equation pair - two electrons gained must equal two lost.

check.stem: In 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl, the chlorine is

options.text: The oxidising agent, reduced from 0 to -1 as each atom gains an electron
options.explanation: Chlorine takes the electrons sodium loses, which is reduction and hence oxidising behaviour.

options.text: The reducing agent, oxidised from 0 to -1
options.explanation: Gaining electrons is reduction; the agent that causes oxidation is itself reduced.

options.text: Oxidised, losing electrons to sodium
options.explanation: Electron flow runs from sodium to chlorine, not the reverse.

options.text: A catalyst that speeds the metal's oxidation
options.explanation: Chlorine is consumed into the salt, so it is a reactant.

check.stem: Calcium reacting with bromine forms CaBr2 because

options.text: Each calcium atom loses two electrons, needing two bromine atoms to accept one each
options.explanation: Ca -> Ca2+ + 2e- pairs with Br2 + 2e- -> 2Br-, giving the 1:2 formula.

options.text: Bromine donates two electrons to calcium
options.explanation: The halogen is the electron acceptor in these reactions.

options.text: Calcium is a Group 1 metal with one valence electron
options.explanation: Calcium is Group 2 and loses two electrons.

options.text: Two bromine atoms share their electrons with calcium covalently
options.explanation: The product is ionic, not covalent.

check.stem: Iodine fails to oxidise iron(II) because

options.text: Its electron capture is too weak to pull Fe2+ up to Fe3+
options.explanation: The oxidising power of iodine falls short of the iron(III)/iron(II) pull.

options.text: Iodine molecules cannot accept any electrons at all
options.explanation: Iodine accepts electrons from stronger reducing agents; it is just too weak for Fe2+.

options.text: Iron(II) ions repel iodine molecules
options.explanation: No repulsion argument applies; the thermodynamics of electron capture decides.

options.text: Iron(II) is already fully oxidised
options.explanation: Iron(II) can still rise to iron(III), as chlorine and bromine prove.

check.stem: In Cl2 + 2Fe2+ -> 2Cl- + 2Fe3+, how many electrons move in total?

options.text: Two, one to each chlorine atom, one lost by each iron(II)
options.explanation: Each Fe2+ loses one electron and each chlorine atom gains one, so the ledger closes at two.

options.text: Four, two per chlorine atom
options.explanation: Each chlorine atom gains only one electron to reach -1.

options.text: One, a single electron hops once
options.explanation: Two iron(II) ions are oxidised, so two electrons move.

options.text: None, this is not a redox reaction
options.explanation: Both iron and chlorine change oxidation number, so electrons transfer.

check.stem: Mixing iron(III) solution with potassium iodide gives iodine because

options.text: Iron(III) is a strong enough oxidising agent to take electrons from iodide
options.explanation: Fe3+ oxidises I- to I2 while being reduced to Fe2+, the demonstrated reversal.

options.text: Iodine donates electrons to iron(III)
options.explanation: Iodide loses the electrons; iodine is the product of that oxidation.

options.text: Iron(III) reduces iodide to iodine
options.explanation: Reduction of iodide would keep it as I-, not produce I2.

options.text: The iodide acts as the oxidising agent
options.explanation: The oxidising agent is iron(III); iodide is oxidised.

check.stem: Write the equation for calcium reacting with bromine.
check.modelAnswer: Ca (s) + Br2 (l) -> CaBr2 (s), with calcium oxidised from 0 to +2.

check.stem: State which halogens can oxidise iron(II) to iron(III).
check.modelAnswer: Chlorine and bromine achieve the iron(III) oxidation; iodine cannot.

check.stem: Explain why the halogens are described as oxidising agents in their reactions with metals.
check.modelAnswer: In every such reaction the halogen molecules gain the electrons the metal atoms lose, so the halogen is reduced and the metal oxidised, which is precisely the action of an oxidising agent.

check.stem: A solution of Fe2+ contaminated with I- is treated with chlorine water. State and explain the two redox changes that occur.
check.modelAnswer: Chlorine oxidises both: each Fe2+ loses an electron to become Fe3+, and each I- loses an electron to give brown iodine, while the chlorine is reduced to chloride - two oxidations sharing one reduced reagent.

lessons.title: Disproportionation in cold alkali
lessons.opening: One chlorine molecule, two fates: in cold dilute alkali around 15 degrees Celsius, chlorine splits itself, rising to +1 in chlorate(I) and sinking to -1 in chloride at the same time. That double role is disproportionation.
keyPoints: A disproportionation reaction is one in which the same species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.
In cold dilute alkali chlorine forms chloride and chlorate(I): Cl2 + 2OH- -> Cl- + ClO- + H2O.
The chlorine falling to -1 is reduced; the chlorine rising to +1 in ClO- is oxidised.
The two half-equations together account for every chlorine atom and every electron moved.

low.restatement: Cold alkali splits chlorine into a -1 chloride branch and a +1 chlorate(I) branch, both from the same neutral molecules - self-oxidation and self-reduction in one pot.
low.analogy: A pair of twins leave home together: one moves down the hill to -1, the other climbs to +1, both from the same starting point at 0.
low.examPointer: Show the oxidation-number changes 0 to -1 and 0 to +1 explicitly; naming the product chlorate(I) with its oxidation number earns the explanation mark.

medium.restatement: The electron ledger is internal: the chlorine atom that becomes Cl- gains the electron that the chlorine atom becoming ClO- loses. Hydroxide supplies oxygen and accepts protons, so the ionic equation balances in atoms and charge.
medium.analogy: One atom passes a coin straight to its partner atom; nothing leaves the pair except the shared hydroxide handing over oxygen.
medium.examPointer: Balance the ionic equation in charge too: -2 on the left (two hydroxides) equals -2 on the right (chloride plus chlorate(I)).

check.stem: A disproportionation reaction is one in which

options.text: A single species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced
options.explanation: Disproportionation splits one oxidation state into a higher and a lower one simultaneously.

options.text: Two different species exchange oxidation numbers
options.explanation: That is a normal redox reaction, not disproportionation.

options.text: A species is oxidised without any electron movement
options.explanation: Oxidation always involves electron loss or an equivalent oxidation-number rise.

options.text: A compound splits into its elements
options.explanation: Decomposition into elements is not disproportionation.

check.stem: In Cl2 + 2OH- -> Cl- + ClO- + H2O, the chlorine that becomes ClO- has been

options.text: Oxidised, from 0 to +1
options.explanation: Rising to +1 in chlorate(I) means electron loss, so oxidation.

options.text: Reduced, from 0 to +1
options.explanation: A rise in oxidation number is oxidation, not reduction.

options.text: Neither, because its charge is still negative
options.explanation: The ionic charge and oxidation number are different bookkeeping quantities.

options.text: Hydrated rather than redox-changed
options.explanation: The +1 oxidation state is a genuine redox change.

check.stem: Which change happens to the chlorine that forms Cl- in cold alkali?

options.text: Reduction, from 0 to -1 by gaining one electron
options.explanation: Falling to -1 is electron gain, the reduction branch of the disproportionation.

options.text: Oxidation, from 0 to -1
options.explanation: A falling oxidation number is reduction, not oxidation.

options.text: No change, since -1 is chlorine's usual state
options.explanation: The free chlorine started at 0, so the fall is a real change.

options.text: Displacement of hydroxide from solution
options.explanation: No displacement occurs; the chloride forms by electron gain.

check.stem: The cold-alkali ionic equation balances in charge because

options.text: The two hydroxide ions' -2 charge equals the chloride and chlorate(I) charges combined
options.explanation: -1 + (-1) = -2 on the right matches -2 on the left.

options.text: Water neutralises all charges on both sides
options.explanation: Water is neutral and cannot account for the charged balance.

options.text: Chlorine molecules carry no charge so charges vanish
options.explanation: The charged species on both sides must still balance.

options.text: Both sides sum to zero charge
options.explanation: Both sides carry -2, not zero.

check.stem: Why does temperature matter for chlorine in alkali?

options.text: Different temperatures give different products: cold alkali yields chlorate(I), hot alkali yields chlorate(V)
options.explanation: Around 15 degrees the +1 product forms; around 70 degrees the +5 product takes over.

options.text: Temperature changes only the rate, never the products
options.explanation: For chlorine in alkali the product identity itself changes with temperature.

options.text: Cold alkali prevents any reaction occurring
options.explanation: Cold alkali does react, giving the +1 branch.

options.text: Hot alkali stops disproportionation entirely
options.explanation: Hot alkali still disproportionates, into the +5 branch.

check.stem: Define disproportionation.
check.modelAnswer: A reaction in which one species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, splitting into a higher and a lower oxidation state.

check.stem: Write the ionic equation for chlorine in cold dilute alkali.
Explain how the cold-alkali reaction shows disproportionation of chlorine.
check.modelAnswer: One chlorine atom ends at -1 in chloride and another at +1 in chlorate(I), both from neutral chlorine at 0, so the same species has been reduced and oxidised in the same reaction.

check.stem: A student claims chlorine in cold alkali is purely reduced because chloride forms. Correct the claim using oxidation numbers.
check.modelAnswer: Only half the chlorine is reduced to -1; the other half rises to +1 in chlorate(I), so chlorine as a whole is disproportionated, oxidised and reduced simultaneously.

lessons.title: Disproportionation in hot alkali
lessons.opening: Heat the same alkali to around 70 degrees and chlorine reshapes its split: five of six chlorine atoms sink to chloride while one climbs all the way to +5 in chlorate(V). The electron ledger still closes - five gains match one five-electron climb.
keyPoints: In hot dilute alkali chlorine forms chloride and chlorate(V): 3Cl2 + 6OH- -> 5Cl- + ClO3- + 3H2O.
Five chlorine atoms are reduced from 0 to -1; one chlorine atom is oxidised from 0 to +5.
The one atom losing five electrons balances the five atoms each gaining one electron.
The chlorate(V) product contains chlorine at +5, three units above the chlorate(I) of the cold reaction.

low.restatement: Hot alkali pushes one chlorine per six up to +5 while the other five drop to -1; the ionic equation 3Cl2 + 6OH- -> 5Cl- + ClO3- + 3H2O keeps atoms and charge balanced.
low.analogy: Five workers each take one coin while one worker dumps five coins, so the total money moved matches perfectly.
low.examPointer: Always show the 5 = 5 electron ledger (five single gains versus one five-electron loss) when explaining the hot-alkali disproportionation.

medium.restatement: Oxidation numbers certify the branches: 0 to -1 five times, 0 to +5 once. Chlorate(V), ClO3-, carries three oxygens at -2 around one chlorine at +5, fitting the -1 ion charge. The extra oxygen comes from the doubled hydroxide supply.
medium.analogy: A taller ladder needs more rungs: the +5 chlorine carries more oxygen atoms to support its higher oxidation state.
medium.examPointer: Do not reuse the cold-alkali stoichiometry - the hot equation needs 3Cl2 and 6OH- with 5Cl- and 3H2O.

check.stem: In hot alkali, chlorine's oxidation states after reaction are

options.text: -1 in chloride and +5 in chlorate(V)
options.explanation: Five atoms fall to -1 and one climbs to +5, the hot-alkali pair.

options.text: -1 and +1, as in the cold reaction
options.explanation: The +1 chlorate(I) belongs to cold alkali; heat switches the product to +5.

options.text: -1 and +7, reaching perchlorate
options.explanation: Chlorate(VII) is not formed with dilute hot alkali here.

options.text: 0 throughout, as disproportionation needs no change
options.explanation: Disproportionation requires both a rise and a fall from 0.

check.stem: The electron ledger for 3Cl2 + 6OH- -> 5Cl- + ClO3- + 3H2O closes because

options.text: Five chlorine atoms each gain one electron while one chlorine atom loses five
options.explanation: 5 x 1 gained equals 1 x 5 lost, so the transfer is balanced.

options.text: Each chlorine atom both gains and loses five electrons
options.explanation: Each atom takes exactly one branch, not both.

options.text: Hydroxide ions donate the missing five electrons
options.explanation: Hydroxide supplies oxygen and charge balance, not the redox electrons.

options.text: Water absorbs the extra electrons at the end
options.explanation: Water is a product, not an electron sink.

check.stem: Chlorate(V), ClO3-, contains chlorine with oxidation number

options.text: +5, since three oxygens at -2 plus +5 gives the -1 ion charge
+1, matching the cold-alkali product
options.explanation: That is chlorate(I), ClO-, a different ion.

options.text: +3, halfway between the branches
options.explanation: No chlorine(III) product appears in these equations.

options.text: -1, like all chlorine products
options.explanation: The chlorate(V) chlorine is oxidised, not reduced.

check.stem: How many hydroxide ions appear in the hot-alkali ionic equation per 3 chlorine molecules?

options.text: Six, supplying the oxygen atoms for chlorate(V) and the water
options.explanation: 6OH- provides the three oxygens of ClO3- and the three waters.

options.text: Two, exactly as in the cold-alkali equation
options.explanation: The cold equation's 2OH- does not carry enough oxygen for the hot products.

options.text: Five, one per chloride formed
options.explanation: Chloride needs no oxygen; the six hydroxides feed the oxide count.

options.text: Three, one per water formed
options.explanation: Three waters are formed but six hydroxides are consumed.

check.stem: Compared with the cold reaction, the hot reaction differs chiefly in

options.text: The oxidation state of the oxidised chlorine: +5 instead of +1
options.explanation: Heat shifts the disproportionation branch from chlorate(I) to chlorate(V).

options.text: The oxidation state of the reduced chlorine: -3 instead of -1
options.explanation: The reduced branch is still chloride at -1 in both.

options.text: Whether disproportionation happens at all
options.explanation: Both temperatures give disproportionation; only the products differ.

options.text: The role of water as a product
options.explanation: Water forms in both ionic equations.

check.stem: Write the ionic equation for chlorine in hot dilute alkali.
State the oxidation-number changes chlorine undergoes in hot alkali.
check.modelAnswer: Five atoms fall from 0 to -1 in chloride and one atom rises from 0 to +5 in chlorate(V).

check.stem: Show that the hot-alkali equation is a disproportionation using electron counting.
check.modelAnswer: Of the six chlorine atoms, five each gain one electron (0 to -1) and one loses five electrons (0 to +5); five gained equals five lost, so chlorine is both reduced and oxidised.

check.stem: Predict, with reasoning, how many chlorate(V) ions form from 6 Cl2 molecules in excess hot alkali.
check.modelAnswer: 6 Cl2 holds 12 chlorine atoms; one in six is oxidised, so 2 chlorate(V) ions form alongside 10 chloride ions, keeping the five-to-one ratio.

lessons.title: Chlorine water: drinking-water sterilisation
lessons.opening: Chlorine keeps drinking water safe by reacting with water itself: one chlorine molecule splits into hydrochloric acid and chloric(I) acid, another disproportionation. The +1 branch, as HClO and its ClO- ion, kills bacteria and sterilises the supply.
keyPoints: Chlorine reacts with water in a disproportionation, forming HCl and HClO.
The chlorine reduced to -1 ends in hydrochloric acid; the chlorine oxidised to +1 ends in chloric(I) acid.
Chloric(I) acid sterilises water by killing bacteria, and dissociates to H+ and ClO-, which also acts as a sterilising agent.

low.restatement: In water, chlorine becomes both HCl (-1) and HClO (+1); the oxidised branch does the germ-killing, and its dissociation product ClO- keeps sterilising.
low.analogy: One soldier splits into a medic and a guard: the guard (+1 branch) patrols the water killing bacteria while the other simply dissolves.
low.examPointer: Name chloric(I) acid and the ClO- ion when asked how chlorine treats water - both are the sterilising species.

medium.restatement: The equilibrium HClO <=> H+ + ClO- spreads the +1 chlorine across two sterilising forms; both attack bacterial structure, which is why chlorination protects supplies even at low dose.
medium.analogy: A key that exists in two shapes can still open the same lock twice as often.
medium.examPointer: Link 'kills bacteria' to the +1 chlorine species, not to chloride, in water-treatment answers.

check.stem: When chlorine reacts with water, the products are

options.text: Hydrochloric acid and chloric(I) acid
options.explanation: HCl and HClO form as chlorine is reduced and oxidised simultaneously.

options.text: Chloride and chlorate(V) ions only
options.explanation: That pair belongs to alkali conditions, not pure water.

options.text: Hydrogen and chlorine oxide gases
options.explanation: No gas evolution is the chemistry here; both products stay dissolved.

options.text: Sodium chloride and water
options.explanation: Sodium is not present in chlorine water.

check.stem: The chlorine that ends in HClO has been

options.text: Oxidised from 0 to +1
options.explanation: Rising to +1 in the acid is the oxidation branch of the water disproportionation.

options.text: Reduced from 0 to +1
options.explanation: An oxidation-number rise is oxidation.

options.text: Unchanged, since HClO is neutral
options.explanation: Molecule neutrality does not fix the atom's oxidation number at 0.

options.text: Displaced from solution by the water
options.explanation: No displacement happens; chlorine reacts with the water itself.

check.stem: Why does chloric(I) acid sterilise water?

options.text: It kills bacteria in the water
options.explanation: The +1 chlorine species is the bactericide that makes the supply safe.

options.text: It neutralises all dissolved salts
options.explanation: Sterilisation targets microbes, not salt content.

options.text: It raises the boiling point of the water
options.explanation: Boiling point is irrelevant to disinfection.

options.text: It removes chlorine from the water again
options.explanation: The acid IS the chlorine treatment, not its removal.

check.stem: HClO dissociating in water gives

options.text: H+ and ClO-, and the chlorate(I) ion also sterilises
options.explanation: The dissociation spreads the +1 chlorine into a second active species.

options.text: H+ and Cl-, completing reduction
options.explanation: Cl- is the -1 branch, not the dissociation of HClO.

options.text: H2 and O2, decomposing to elements
options.explanation: No such decomposition occurs in solution.

options.text: HCl and hydroxide
options.explanation: That would reverse the disproportionation.

check.stem: Which statement about chlorine in water is correct?

options.text: Chlorine is both oxidised and reduced, so the reaction is disproportionation
options.explanation: The 0 state splits into -1 (HCl) and +1 (HClO), the defining pattern.

options.text: Chlorine only dissolves physically, without reaction
options.explanation: Chemical disproportionation occurs, not mere dissolution.

options.text: Only reduction of chlorine occurs in water
options.explanation: The +1 branch proves oxidation happens too.

options.text: The sterilising species is chloride ion
options.explanation: Chloride is the reduced, inactive branch; HClO and ClO- sterilise.

check.stem: Name the two acids formed when chlorine reacts with water.
State the role of ClO- in treated water.
check.modelAnswer: The chlorate(I) ion acts as a sterilising agent, killing bacteria alongside chloric(I) acid.

check.stem: Explain why treating water with chlorine is a disproportionation reaction.
check.modelAnswer: Chlorine at 0 splits into the -1 state in HCl and the +1 state in HClO, so the same element is simultaneously reduced and oxidised.

check.stem: A water board reduces chlorine dose but must still kill bacteria. Explain why a small dose can remain effective.
check.modelAnswer: The +1 chlorine species are potent bactericides used catalytically in the sense that each HClO/ClO- unit attacks bacteria; even low concentrations maintain a sterilising presence throughout the supply.

glossary.definition: A redox reaction in which a single species is simultaneously reduced and oxidised, splitting into higher and lower oxidation states.
The ClO- ion carrying chlorine at +1, formed in cold alkali and acting as a steriliser in water.
The ClO3- ion carrying chlorine at +5, formed in hot alkali.
The HClO acid formed when chlorine reacts with water; it kills bacteria in drinking water.
